title: Server Actions and Forms
summary: Handle forms and writes with Server Actions: validate input, return errors, update cached data, and secure every action like the public endpoint it is.
intro: Almost every app writes data as well as reading it: a review, an item in a cart, a login. In the React course, a form's action ran in the browser, and saving anything meant calling the Trailhead API from the browser, with a request you kept in step with the form. Next.js lets a form call a function that runs on your server instead, and send back the updated page in the same answer. That function is a Server Action. This lesson shows what one is and what travels over the network when it runs, how forms call actions before and after JavaScript loads, how to check input and send errors back, how to show the change on the page, and how to secure every action, since anyone can call one.

steps.title: What a Server Action is
steps.body:
Reading data in Next.js happens in Server Components, as the data lessons showed. Writing needs a way back: the browser has to tell your server that something happened. A Server Action is that way back. Knowing exactly what it sends over the network makes the rest of this lesson easier to follow, including why every action has to be secured.

## A function the browser can call

A **Server Function**, which the lesson on Server and Client Components named, is an async function that runs on your server and that code in the browser can call over the network. You make one with the `"use server"` directive, a plain string written as the first line of a file or of a function, like the `"use client"` you met in the lesson on Server and Client Components. When a Server Function handles a form or another write, it's called a **Server Action**. That's the name you'll hear most.

Write `"use server"` at the top of a file, and every function the file exports becomes one. This is `app/products/[slug]/actions.ts`:

```ts
"use server";

import { refresh } from "next/cache";
import { apiFetch } from "@/lib/api";

export async function addToCart(slug: string, formData: FormData) {
  const quantity = Number(formData.get("quantity"));
  await apiFetch(`/cart/items/${slug}`, {
    method: "PUT",
    body: JSON.stringify({ quantity }),
    session: true,
  });
  refresh();
}
```

`apiFetch` is the helper in `lib/api.ts` from the lesson on fetching data, and `session: true` makes it forward the visitor's login cookie. The cart belongs to one person, so it's never cached and has no tag to expire. `refresh()` renders the page again instead, so the header's cart count, read fresh on every request, shows the new number, as the caching lesson explained. Part 3 shows how to check input like `quantity` properly.

You can also write `"use server"` as the first line inside an async function in a Server Component, which turns just that one function into an action. A Client Component can't define an action, but it can import one from a `"use server"` file, or receive one as a prop.

## What the build does with it

When Next.js builds your app, it treats an actions file in two ways. On the server, each function stays exactly as you wrote it. In the JavaScript sent to the browser, each function's body is swapped for a **reference**: an **action ID**, a long string Next.js generates for that function, plus a small stand-in that sends a request when it's called. Your code, the API helper, and any secret it reads never leave the server. Only the ID does.

## What travels over the network

Calling an action sends a POST request to the URL of the page you're on. There's no route to write and no new file in `app/`. The request carries:

- A `Next-Action` header holding the action ID, so Next.js knows which function to run.
- An `Accept: text/x-component` header, asking for the answer in the RSC payload format, the description of a rendered tree that Server Components send.
- The arguments in the body: the form's fields, and any values bound to the action.

```diagram server-actions-roundtrip
One request goes out, and one answer brings back the result and the updated page.
```

In step 1, you press Post on the review form. In step 2, Next.js reads the header, finds `createReview`, and runs it with the arguments from the body. The action saves the review and calls `updateTag`. Because cached data changed, step 3 renders the current page again on the server. In step 4, one response carries both the action's return value and the new RSC payload, and React swaps the changed parts into the page in front of you. You don't need a second request to see the new review.

## Arguments and results are serialized

Everything that crosses the network is turned into text and back, which you met as serializing in the lesson on Server and Client Components. Actions follow the same rules as props passed from a Server Component to a Client Component: strings, numbers, booleans, plain objects and arrays, `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, `FormData`, and promises cross, while class instances and ordinary functions don't. Everything an action returns reaches the browser, so return a small object made for the page, like `{ message: "Saved" }`, never a whole database record.

## Where actions live, and what they're for

Keep a feature's actions in one `actions.ts` next to the pages that use them, with `"use server"` at the top. One file per feature is easy to find and easy to review, and it needs reviewing, since every export in it is a door into your server.

Actions are for writes. The browser sends them one at a time, and waits for each to finish before it sends the next, so the page always matches the latest result. That makes them a poor way to read data, which belongs in Server Components.

examples.explanation: The request goes to the page's own path, `/products/trail-pack-45`. The `Next-Action` header names the action by its ID. The body is **multipart** form data, the encoding a file upload uses: each field is its own part, between the boundary lines. React named the form's fields `_1_rating` and `_1_title`. The part named `0` is the list of arguments: `"trail-pack-45"` is the slug bound to the action, `{}` is the previous state, and `$K1` points at the form fields. The response is `text/x-component`. Its line `1:` is the action's return value, and line `0:` carries the page rendered again, cut short here. `x-action-revalidated: 1` tells the router in the browser that cached data changed, so it also drops the copies of other pages it saved while prefetching links.

steps.title: Forms that call actions
steps.body:
A form is the most common way to call an action, and it brings a bonus you know from the web course: an HTML form can send itself with no JavaScript at all. Next.js keeps that working. A slow phone, or a page whose scripts haven't arrived yet, still gets a form that works, and it gets better once JavaScript is ready.

## A form whose action is a function

In a Server Component, pass the action to a form's `action` prop. When the action needs more than the form's fields, fill in its first arguments with `bind`:

```tsx sketch
<form action={addToCart.bind(null, slug)}>
  <input type="hidden" name="quantity" value="1" />
  <button>Add to cart</button>
</form>
```

`bind` is JavaScript's way to make a new function with its first arguments already filled in. The `null` is the value for `this`, which actions don't use, and `slug` becomes the first argument. The form's fields arrive after it, as `FormData`, which is why `addToCart` takes `(slug, formData)`.

## Before JavaScript loads

React renders that form as plain HTML that any browser can send: `method="POST"`, `encType="multipart/form-data"`, and a few hidden inputs whose names start with `$ACTION_`, holding the action ID and the bound arguments. The first example shows the real HTML.

Press the button with JavaScript turned off, and the browser does what it always does with a form: it posts the fields and shows whatever page comes back. Next.js finds the action from the hidden inputs, runs it, and answers with the whole page as HTML, rendered after the write. That's **progressive enhancement**: the page works with HTML alone and improves when JavaScript arrives.

Once the page is hydrated, meaning React has attached its event handlers in the browser, React takes over the submit, sends the request from the previous part instead, and updates the page in place, with no reload. A form in a Client Component that's pressed while its scripts are still loading holds the press, and sends it as soon as React is ready.

## Messages and pending state with useActionState

Most forms need to answer: Saved, or Fix this field. The `useActionState` hook from the React course works with Server Actions. It wraps the action, keeps whatever the action last returned as state, and gives you a `pending` flag while the request is in flight. It's a hook, so it lives in a Client Component, and the action it wraps receives the previous state before the form data: `createReview(slug, previous, formData)`. The second example shows the form.

The product page, a Server Component, binds the slug and hands the action down as a prop:

```tsx sketch
<ReviewForm action={createReview.bind(null, slug)} />
```

Server Functions are the one kind of function you may pass to a Client Component, since only a reference crosses. This form still works without JavaScript, too. React adds one more hidden input, `$ACTION_KEY`, so the state that comes back with the HTML lands in the right form, error messages and all.

For a submit button that shows its own pending state, `useFormStatus` from `react-dom` reads the status of the form the button sits in, so one `SubmitButton` component works in every form.

## Two actions in one form

A button's `formAction` prop replaces the form's action for that button alone. A post editor can have a Save draft button with `formAction={saveDraft}` next to a Publish button that uses the form's own action.

## Search forms with next/form

Some forms change nothing on the server. A search box only changes the URL, like `/search?q=tent`, and the page reads it from `searchParams`. For those, `next/form` gives you a `Form` component: `<Form action="/search">` sends a GET with its fields in the query string, just like an HTML form. Next.js also prefetches the search page's loading UI while the form is on screen, and when you submit, it moves to the results without reloading the page, so the layout and its state stay put. Without JavaScript, it's an ordinary GET form.

The `$ACTION_` inputs are React's. `$ACTION_0:0` names the action by its ID and says its bound arguments are in another field, and `$ACTION_0:1` holds them: `["trail-pack-45"]`, the slug from `bind`. `"` is the character reference for a double quote. examples.title: A review form with useActionState
examples.prompt: `app/products/[slug]/review-form.tsx`, a Client Component that shows the action's messages, field errors, and pending state.
examples.explanation: `useActionState(action, {})` starts with an empty object as the state. `formAction` is what the form calls: it sends the previous state and the form's fields to the Server Action, and stores what comes back as the new `state`. While the request is in flight, `pending` is `true`, so the button turns off and says Posting. Each field's error shows under it, and the message goes in an `aria-live` paragraph, which screen readers announce when it changes. React clears a form's fields after its action finishes, so the action sends back what was typed in `state.values`, and each field uses it as its `defaultValue`. A failed submit keeps the words, and a successful one, which sends no values, leaves the form empty.

steps.title: Validating input and returning errors
steps.body:
The checks a form makes in the browser, like `required` or `type="email"`, help honest visitors. They don't stop anyone else. An action is reached by a POST request, and anyone can send one with whatever fields they like, as part 5 shows with `curl`. So every action checks its input again on the server, and sends back errors the form can show.

## Read the fields, then check them

`formData.get(name)` returns the field's value, or `null` when the field is missing. Every value from a form is a string, even a number like a rating. `Object.fromEntries(formData)` turns all the fields into one object, but in an action it also holds React's `$ACTION_` fields, so pick the fields you want by name.

A **zod schema**, which you met in the React course, says what valid input looks like and checks it in one call:

```ts
const ReviewInput = z.object({
  rating: z.coerce.number().int().min(1, "Pick a rating").max(5),
  title: z.string().trim().min(1, "Give your review a title").max(80),
  body: z.string().trim().min(1, "Write a few words about it").max(2000, "Keep it under 2,000 characters"),
});
```

`z.coerce.number()` turns the string `"4"` into the number 4 before checking it. `.trim()` removes spaces at both ends, so a title of only spaces counts as empty. The rules match the Trailhead API's own for a review: a rating from 1 to 5, a title of 1 to 80 characters, and a body of 1 to 2,000. The messages are the words your form shows.

`safeParse` checks without throwing. It returns `success: true` with the clean `data`, or `success: false` with an `error`. `z.flattenError(error).fieldErrors` turns that error into one list of messages per field, like `{ title: ["Give your review a title"] }`, which is exactly what the form from the previous part reads.

## Expected errors are returned, surprises are thrown

Two kinds of things go wrong in an action, and they're handled differently:

- **Expected errors** are part of normal use: a missing title, a review that already exists, a product that's sold out. Return them as state, so the form can show them next to the fields.
- **Unexpected errors** are bugs and outages: the API is down, or a value is impossible. Throw them. Next.js shows the nearest `error.tsx`, the error page from the routing lesson.

The Trailhead API answers with problem details, the error format from the React course, and the action maps each status to one of those two kinds. A `409 Conflict` means you already reviewed this product, which is expected, so it becomes a message. A `401 Unauthorized` means the visitor isn't logged in, so the action sends them to the login page. Anything else is thrown.

## redirect() throws

`redirect("/login")` from `next/navigation` doesn't return. It works by throwing a special error that Next.js catches and turns into a redirect, so the code after it never runs. That's why it can't sit inside a `try` block: your own `catch` would catch it first. Call it after the `try`, or in the `catch`, as the example does. In an action called from JavaScript, the redirect comes back as an `x-action-redirect` header and the router moves to the new page. Without JavaScript, the browser gets an ordinary redirect.

## Never trust the client

Everything in the request came from the browser, and the browser is under the visitor's control. That includes more than the visible fields:

- **Bound arguments** sit in the page as plain text, as the previous part's HTML showed. The slug here is checked against the pattern the Trailhead API uses for slugs, `^[a-z0-9-]+$`, before it goes into a URL. Without that check, a slug like `../me` would send the request to a different API path.
- **Hidden fields** are just as easy to change. Never take a price, an owner, or a role from the form. Send an ID, and read the rest on the server.
- **Who the visitor is** comes from the session cookie, read on the server, never from a field. The lesson on secrets and auth builds that.

Validating checks that input has the right shape. It doesn't check that the visitor is allowed to do the thing. That's the job of part 5.

examples.title: The review action, checked
examples.prompt: `app/products/[slug]/actions.ts`: the action behind the review form, which checks the slug and the fields, maps the API's errors, and expires the cached reviews.
examples.explanation: The action takes the bound slug, the previous state that `useActionState` passes in, and the form data. `Slug.parse` throws on a slug that doesn't match the pattern, since a bad slug means someone changed the page, not that someone made a typo, and a thrown error goes to `error.tsx`. The fields are read one by one, turned into strings, and kept in `values` to send back. A failed `safeParse` returns the field errors with those values, and the API is never called. `ApiError` is the error `apiFetch` throws for an answer that isn't a 2xx, with the status on it. A 401 redirects to the login page, with a `next` parameter so login can send the visitor back. A 409 becomes a message. Anything else is rethrown. Only after the review is saved does `updateTag` expire the cached reviews, which the next part explains.

steps.title: Showing the change on the page
steps.body:
After a write, the page has to show it: the new review in the list, the new count in the cart. Two things stand in the way. The server's caches still hold the old data, and the round trip to the server takes time. This part handles both: expiring the right cache from the action, and showing the change at once while the request is still in flight.

## Expire what the action changed

The caching lesson cached the product page's reviews with `cacheTag(`reviews-${slug}`)`. Unless the action says so, that cache keeps serving the old list after a new review is saved. Next.js gives you four ways to say so, all from `next/cache`:

| Call | What it does | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `updateTag(tag)` | expires the tag now, so the next read waits for fresh data | visitors must see their own change at once |
| `revalidateTag(tag, "max")` | marks the tag stale, serving the old copy while a fresh one loads in the background | the change comes from elsewhere, like a webhook |
| `revalidatePath(path)` | expires what's cached for one URL | one page changed and has no tag |
| `refresh()` | renders the current page again without expiring anything | the page shows uncached data, like a count read on every request |

`updateTag` and `refresh` work only inside Server Actions. The other two also work in Route Handlers, which the next lesson covers.

## One round trip

When an action calls `updateTag`, `revalidatePath`, or `refresh`, sets or deletes a cookie, or calls `redirect`, Next.js renders the current page again before it answers, and sends the new RSC payload in the same response as the return value. That's step 3 in the diagram in the first part. `revalidateTag` with `"max"` is the exception: it doesn't render again in the response, so the change shows up on a later visit. That fits a change someone else made, and doesn't fit a visitor waiting to see their own review.

Order matters inside the action. Expire tags before you call `redirect`, since nothing after `redirect` runs. Expire them after the write succeeds, never before, or the page renders again while the old data is still there.

## Show it before the server answers

Even one round trip takes a moment, and on a phone it can be most of a second. `useOptimistic`, from the React course, shows the result you expect right away, and lets the server's answer replace it.

It fits Server Actions well because of how the answer arrives. The reviews list is a Client Component that gets the server's reviews as a prop. `useOptimistic(reviews, add)` returns a list that also holds any reviews you add while an action runs. When the action finishes, its response brings the page rendered again, so the prop now holds the real review, and the optimistic copy is dropped. You don't merge anything by hand.

## Rollback is automatic

An optimistic value lasts only while its action runs. If the action fails, or returns an error like "You already reviewed this product", the page comes back without a new review in the prop, the action ends, and the optimistic copy disappears by itself. That's the **rollback**: the page returns to what the server says is true. Always show why, with the message the action returned, so the visitor isn't left wondering where their review went.

The example combines both hooks. The function given to `useActionState` first adds the optimistic review, then awaits the Server Action and returns its state. It runs inside a **transition**, React's name for an update that can take its time, which is the one place optimistic updates are allowed.

Try it logged in as Sam. The review appears at once with the author You, then turns into the server's copy, by Sam, when the answer comes back. Post a second review of the same product and the API answers `409`: the review shows by You for a moment, then vanishes, and the message says you already reviewed it, with your words still in the form.

examples.title: An optimistic reviews list
examples.prompt: `app/products/[slug]/reviews.tsx`: the reviews list and its form in one Client Component, showing a new review before the server answers.
examples.explanation: `useOptimistic` takes the real list and a function that says how to add one item. `shown` is what the page draws: the real list, plus anything added while an action runs. The function given to `useActionState` calls `addShown` with a review built from the form, marked with the id `pending` and the author You, then awaits the Server Action and returns its state. `aria-busy` tells screen readers that item is still being saved. When the action's response arrives, `reviews` holds the real review and `shown` follows it. When the action returns an error instead, `shown` falls back to `reviews`, which never got the new one, and the message explains why. The page passes `reviews` and `createReview.bind(null, slug)` as props.

steps.title: Securing every action
steps.body:
An action feels like a function you call from your own page. On the network it's an HTTP endpoint that takes POST requests, and anyone can send one, from any program, with any fields. Your form is only one way in. So every action has to check who's calling and whether they're allowed, the same way an API endpoint would.

## Anyone can call it

The first example calls the review action with `curl`, a program that isn't a browser and never loaded your page. It only needs the action ID, which is in the page's HTML for anyone to read. The action ran: it called the API, got a 401 because there was no session cookie, and answered with its own redirect to the login page. If `createReview` had written to a database directly, with no check of its own, that `curl` would have posted a review.

## Check inside every action

Put the checks at the top of each action, before it does anything:

- **Authenticate**: find out who's calling, from the session cookie, read on the server. With no session, stop.
- **Authorize**: check that this visitor may do this thing to this item. Being logged in isn't enough to delete a review, or to change an order. You have to own it. Skipping this second check is a well-known bug called an **insecure direct object reference**, or IDOR: change the ID in a request, and you reach someone else's data.

A check on the page doesn't cover its actions. A page that redirects visitors who aren't logged in still has actions anyone can POST to, because the action is its own way in. The lesson on secrets and auth builds a `verifySession()` helper and a data access layer that make these checks hard to forget.

## What Next.js does for you

Next.js adds a few protections of its own:

- **POST only.** An action never runs from a GET, so a link or an image can't trigger one.
- **An origin check.** Next.js compares the request's `Origin` header, which browsers add to say which site sent it, with the host the request came in on. When they don't match, it refuses. That stops another site from making your visitor's browser post to your actions with your visitor's cookies, the cross-site request forgery from the React course. The second example shows the refusal. When your app sits behind another server that passes requests on under a different name, like a CDN, list the extra names in `experimental.serverActions.allowedOrigins` in `next.config.ts`.
- **A size limit.** An action's request body is capped at 1 MB. Raise it with `experimental.serverActions.bodySizeLimit` when an action takes uploads.
- **Only used actions get IDs.** An exported action that nothing calls is left out of the build, so it has no ID and can't be reached.
- **Encrypted closures.** An action written inside a component can use that component's variables, which is called a **closure**. Next.js sends those variables to the browser and back encrypted, with a key made for each build and saved with it, so servers running copies of one build agree. Servers that build the app separately must share a key, `NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, which the deployment lesson sets up. Values passed with `bind` are not encrypted: they're in the page as plain text, as the forms part showed.

Notice what the origin check doesn't do. A request from `curl`, or from any script, has no `Origin` header, or any `Origin` it likes, so it gets through. The check protects your visitors' browsers. It does nothing to stop someone calling your action directly, which is why your own checks come first.

## Limit what can be abused

Some actions cost you each time they run: sending an email, charging a card, calling a paid API. Count calls per visitor or per address, and refuse past a limit. Keep the count in a shared store, such as your database or Redis, a fast store that keeps its data in memory, since an app running on several servers can't count in one server's own memory. And return only what the page needs, since a return value reaches the browser like everything else.

Next.js aborted the action before it ran and answered 500. The body's line `1:` is an error with only a digest, the short code from the routing lesson that matches the full error in the server's log, so no details leak to the caller. The terminal running `next start` printed the reason: `x-forwarded-host` header with value `127.0.0.1:3005` does not match `origin` header with value `evil.example` from a forwarded Server Actions request. Aborting the action. Then it printed Error: Invalid Server Actions request, with the same digest. Server Actions answer your own pages' forms. The next lesson covers the requests that come from everywhere else, with Route Handlers, and the code that sees every request first, proxy.

recap:
- A Server Action is an async function marked "use server" that the browser calls with a POST to the current page's URL.
- The browser gets only an action ID, and one response brings back the return value and, after a write, the page rendered again.
